title: CPR (Adult & Older Child)
short_desc: Emergency lifesaving procedure performed when the heart stops beating.
steps: Check for safety and responsiveness. Tap the shoulder and shout, 'Are you okay?'
Call emergency services immediately if there is no response.
Check for breathing. If they are not breathing or only gasping, begin CPR.
Place the heel of one hand in the center of the chest, place the other hand on top, and interlock fingers.
Push hard and fast: at least 2 inches deep, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions a minute.
Continue compressions until emergency medical help arrives or the person starts breathing.
warnings: Do not attempt rescue breaths if you are not trained; hands-only CPR is highly effective.
Never practice CPR on a healthy, breathing person.

title: Choking (Heimlich Maneuver)
short_desc: Action to take if an adult or child is clutching their throat and cannot breathe or cough.
steps: Ask 'Are you choking?' If they nod yes and cannot talk, act immediately.
Stand behind the person and wrap your arms around their waist.
Make a fist with one hand and place the thumb side just above the person's belly button.
Grasp your fist with your other hand.
Give quick, upward thrusts into the abdomen as if trying to lift the person up.
Repeat until the blockage is dislodged or the person becomes unconscious.
warnings: If the person becomes unconscious, lower them to the ground and begin CPR.
Do not perform blind finger sweeps in the mouth; you may push the object deeper.

title: Heart Attack Symptoms
short_desc: Recognizing and reacting to suspected cardiac arrest or heart attack.
steps: Call emergency services immediately. Do not ignore the symptoms.
Have the person sit down, rest, and try to keep them calm.
Loosen any tight clothing.
If the person is conscious and not allergic, have them chew and swallow an aspirin.
If the person falls unconscious and stops breathing, begin CPR immediately.
warnings: Do not let the person drive themselves to the hospital.
Do not wait to see if the symptoms go away.

title: Seizures / Epilepsy
short_desc: What to do if someone is experiencing a sudden, uncontrolled electrical disturbance in the brain.
steps: Ease the person to the floor and place something soft under their head.
Turn the person gently onto one side. This helps them breathe.
Clear the area of hard or sharp objects.
Remove eyeglasses and loosen ties or anything around the neck.
Time the seizure. If it lasts longer than 5 minutes, call an ambulance.
warnings: Do not hold the person down or try to stop their movements.
Do not put anything in the person's mouth (they will not swallow their tongue).

title: Severe Bleeding / Deep Cuts
short_desc: Stopping heavy blood loss from deep cuts or trauma.
steps: Apply direct, firm pressure to the wound with a clean cloth, tissue, or piece of clothing.
If blood soaks through, do not remove the cloth. Add more layers on top and keep pressing.
Elevate the injured area above the heart if possible.
If the bleeding doesn't stop after 15 minutes of continuous pressure, seek emergency help.
Keep the person warm to prevent shock.
warnings: Do not use a tourniquet unless you are trained to do so and the bleeding is life-threatening and uncontrollable.
Do not remove objects embedded in the wound; apply pressure around the object.

title: Snake Bite
short_desc: Emergency response to a venomous or unknown snake bite.
steps: Move away from the snake to prevent further bites.
Keep the victim calm and still. Movement causes venom to spread faster.
Remove rings, watches, or tight clothing around the bitten limb before swelling starts.
Keep the bitten limb at or slightly below the level of the heart.
Call emergency services immediately.
warnings: Do NOT cut the wound or attempt to suck the venom out.
Do NOT apply a tourniquet, ice, or submerge the wound in water.
Do not give the person caffeine or alcohol.

title: Burns (Thermal)
short_desc: Immediate action for heat-related burns from fire, hot liquids, or steam.
steps: Remove the person from the heat source immediately.
Cool the burn under cool (not cold or ice) running water for 10 to 20 minutes.
Remove rings, tight items, or clothing near the burned area before swelling occurs.
Cover the burn loosely with a sterile, non-stick dressing or clean cloth.
Take an over-the-counter pain reliever if necessary and if you have no allergies.
warnings: Never apply ice, butter, toothpaste, or ointments to a severe burn.
Do not pop blisters.
Seek immediate medical help if the burn covers a large area, involves the face/hands, or looks charred.

title: Fractures / Broken Bones
short_desc: First aid for suspected bone fractures or severe dislocations.
steps: Do not move the injured person unless there is immediate danger.
Stop any bleeding by applying pressure to the wound with a sterile bandage or clean cloth.
Immobilize the injured area. Do not try to realign the bone or push a bone that's sticking out back in.
Apply ice packs to limit swelling and help relieve pain. Don't apply ice directly to the skin.
Treat for shock. If the person feels faint, lay them down and elevate their legs slightly.
warnings: If it's a suspected neck or back injury, do NOT move the person at all. Wait for paramedics.

title: Heat Stroke
short_desc: Life-threatening heat illness caused by body overheating.
steps: Move the person to a cool, shaded, or air-conditioned environment immediately.
Call emergency services. Heat stroke is a medical emergency.
Remove unnecessary clothing.
Cool the person rapidly by spraying with cool water, fanning, or placing ice packs in the armpits, groin, and neck.
If the person is fully conscious, give them cool water to drink.
warnings: If the person is confused, vomiting, or unconscious, do not give them anything to drink.

title: Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia)
short_desc: Quick treatment for someone experiencing sudden drops in blood sugar (often diabetic).
steps: If the person is conscious and can swallow, give them 15-20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates.
Good sources: A glass of fruit juice, regular (non-diet) soda, 1 tablespoon of honey, or hard candies.
Wait 15 minutes and check how they feel. If symptoms persist, give another 15g of carbs.
Once they feel better, have them eat a small snack with complex carbs and protein (e.g., half a sandwich).
warnings: If the person is unconscious or having a seizure, do NOT force food or fluids into their mouth. Call an ambulance.

title: Asthma Attack
short_desc: First aid for sudden shortness of breath and wheezing.
steps: Sit the person upright comfortably and loosen any tight clothing.
Help them use their prescribed reliever inhaler (usually blue) with a spacer if available.
Instruct them to take 1 puff every 30-60 seconds, up to a maximum of 10 puffs.
If symptoms do not improve after 10 puffs, or if you are worried, call an ambulance.
If the ambulance takes longer than 15 minutes, repeat the inhaler steps.
warnings: Do not lay the person flat; this restricts breathing further.

title: High Fever (Adults)
short_desc: Management of elevated body temperature without immediate access to a doctor.
steps: Rest and drink plenty of fluids (water, oral rehydration solutions, clear broths).
Take over-the-counter fever reducers like Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) as per package instructions.
Dress in lightweight clothing and use a light blanket if shivering.
Apply a lukewarm (not cold) damp sponge or cloth to the forehead and armpits.
warnings: Do not use cold baths or alcohol rubs; they can cause shivering, which raises core temperature.
Seek emergency care if fever is accompanied by severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, or breathing difficulty.

title: Food Poisoning / Diarrhea
short_desc: Managing symptoms of contaminated food consumption.
steps: Stay hydrated. Drink plenty of clear fluids, primarily ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) or water with a pinch of salt and sugar.
Eat bland foods (BRAT diet: Bananas, Rice, Applesauce, Toast) when you feel ready.
Rest adequately as your body flushes the toxins.
Avoid caffeine, dairy products, alcohol, and greasy or heavily seasoned foods.
warnings: Do not immediately take anti-diarrheal medication; letting the body expel the bacteria is often better initially.
Seek medical help if you cannot keep liquids down for 24 hours, have a high fever, or notice blood in stool.

title: Nosebleed
short_desc: Stopping common nosebleeds quickly and safely.
steps: Sit upright and lean slightly forward (NOT backward).
Pinch the soft part of your nose shut against the hard bony ridge that forms the bridge of the nose.
Breathe through your mouth and keep pinching for 10 to 15 minutes continuously.
Apply a cold compress or ice pack to the bridge of your nose.
If bleeding doesn't stop after 20 minutes of continuous pressure, seek medical help.
warnings: Do NOT tilt your head back. This causes blood to drain down your throat, which can cause choking or vomiting.
Do not blow your nose for several hours after the bleeding stops.

title: Sprains & Strains
short_desc: Initial treatment for twisted ankles, tweaked knees, or pulled muscles.
steps: REST: Avoid using the injured joint or muscle.
ICE: Apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel for 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours.
COMPRESS: Wrap the injured area with an elastic bandage to reduce swelling (not too tight).
ELEVATE: Keep the injured area raised above heart level if possible.
warnings: Do not apply heat during the first 48 hours, as it can increase swelling.
If you cannot bear any weight or the joint looks deformed, suspect a fracture and seek an X-ray.
